evidence.title: Streamlining organ donation: impact of an artificial intelligence-based protocol post-brain death
evidence.outcome: Time from first apnoea test to organ retrieval before versus after AI protocol implementation
evidence.effect: Retrieval time rose from 1587 (IQR 1328-1779) min pre-AI to 1660 (IQR 1556-1959) min post-AI (p=0.04). Transfer to the operating room after legal verification rose from 125 to 384 min (p=0.002).

evidence.sample_unit: deceased organ donor cases (declared dead by neurological criteria)

commentary.bottom_line: No study tested whether piloting AI with structured monitoring of workflow, safety, and workforce effects prevents harm when a tool is scaled, so support for R112 rests on six endorsements from frameworks and commentaries. Four hazard studies show that workflow problems can appear or be absent during real deployments, which suggests that local pilot monitoring may be informative.

perspectives.view: Zero studies compare piloting with monitoring against scaling without it. The four hazard studies describe workflow outcomes during single deployments. Two found problems and two found none, and their designs range from one randomized trial to uncontrolled pre-post and survey data. These studies establish that the hazard varies by setting, but they cannot estimate the effect of the recommended practice.

In 45 organ donor cases in India, time from first apnoea test to retrieval rose from 1587 to 1660 minutes after an AI protocol began (p=0.04). Transfer to the operating room after legal verification rose from 125 to 384 minutes (p=0.002). This suggests that downstream delays can follow AI adoption, and monitoring may detect them before wider spread.

A US randomized trial of 536 encounters reported low accrual and workflow integration problems, including difficulty reaching the right person at the right time. By contrast, 81% of 59 staff in another deployment disagreed that their workflow was disrupted, and a four-center trauma pilot reported no disruption. Integration results appear to depend on local workflow, which supports testing at each site.

The trauma pilot enrolled 139 of 391 eligible patients over three months at four centers, and the US trial reported low accrual. These figures suggest that pilots may reach only part of the eligible population. Workflow findings from a partial pilot may therefore understate the burden that appears at full volume.

None of the four hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two did not report their country. A pilot that finds no workflow disruption in the studied settings gives no information about settings with fewer staff or more interpreter-dependent encounters.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare sites that scale AI after a monitored pilot with sites that scale without one, measuring workflow disruption, staff burden, safety events, and downstream delays after full rollout. Pilots should also report how representative enrolled patients and staff are of the eventual deployment population.
commentary.underserved_note: No hazard study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice itself. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that pilot findings from other settings apply, and they may need to include these groups in their own pilot monitoring.
